items.title: The Bay of Pigs invasion (April 1961) was a CIA-trained failure
items.claim: What happened at the Bay of Pigs?

options.text: A successful US Marine landing in Cuba

Around 1,400 CIA-trained Cuban exiles (Brigade 2506) landed at Bahía de Cochinos on 17 April 1961; without expected US air support, they were defeated within three days, with 114 killed and around 1,200 captured
A peaceful protest broken up by Castro's police

items.reveal:
The operation was planned under Eisenhower and inherited by Kennedy after his January 1961 inauguration. Kennedy cancelled the second air strike that would have neutralised Cuban air power. The exiles landed in swampy terrain with no popular uprising materialising.

Kennedy publicly accepted responsibility — 'success has many fathers, failure is an orphan' — and the CIA director Allen Dulles resigned. The prisoners were exchanged in December 1962 for $53 million of food and medicine.

The humiliation pushed Castro further toward the Soviet Union; Khrushchev's decision to place missiles in Cuba in 1962 followed directly. Operation Mongoose continued covert efforts against Castro through the 1960s.
items.why: Failed interventions can be more consequential than successful ones. The Bay of Pigs led directly to the Cuban Missile Crisis — and reshaped Cold War risk-taking for both sides.

items.title: Most Roman emperors died violently
items.claim: Of the 69 Roman emperors from Augustus (27 BCE) to Theodosius I (395 CE), how many died of natural causes?

options.text: Almost all — emperors were generally well-protected
Roughly a third — the rest died by assassination, in battle, by suicide or under suspicious circumstances
All emperors after Nero were murdered

items.reveal:
Joseph Saleh and colleagues (2019) modelled imperial deaths and found violent end rates above 50% for the first 25 years of any reign. The Crisis of the Third Century (235-284) saw around 50 emperors and usurpers in 50 years.

Named assassinations: Caligula (41), Claudius (54, probably poisoned by Agrippina), Domitian (96), Commodus (192), Caracalla (217), Elagabalus (222) and many more. Some died in war (Decius at Abrittus, 251; Valerian captured by the Persians, 260).
items.why: The imperial succession looks orderly from the list of names. Statistically, becoming emperor was one of the most dangerous jobs in the ancient world — which itself shaped imperial policy.

items.title: Thomas More's 'Utopia' (1516) coined the word
items.claim: What did Thomas More publish in 1516?

options.text: A history of the Wars of the Roses

'Utopia' — a Latin work describing a fictional island society, coining the word from Greek 'ou-topos' (no place) and 'eu-topos' (good place); a humanist critique of European politics, property and religion
A defence of the medieval feudal system

items.reveal_title: No place that critiques every place
items.reveal:
'Utopia' was written in Latin and first printed at Louvain in 1516. The Utopians hold property in common, work six hours a day, practise religious toleration and choose elected officials. The book mixes serious proposal with deliberate ambiguity — More may or may not endorse his fictional society.

More was Lord Chancellor under Henry VIII from 1529 to 1532, resigning over the king's annulment plans. He refused the Oath of Succession (1534) and was executed on 6 July 1535 with the famous 'King's good servant, but God's first.'

He was canonised in 1935. The word 'utopia' entered every European language as a term for an imagined ideal society.
items.why: Renaissance humanism produced political ideas centuries ahead of their reception. 'Utopia' has been read by socialists, anarchists, Catholics and modern progressives — each finding their own programme in More's deliberately ambiguous text.
